choices: Run two instances in one AZ behind an ALB
Spread instances across multiple AZs with an ALB and Auto Scaling
Move the instances to a single larger instance
Add a second region with manual DNS failover
evidence:

scenarios.situation: A 2.5-hour AZ power event took down an entire application because all instances lived in the failed AZ.
scenarios.title: The AZ that took everything
scenarios.why: Multi-AZ deployment across independent Availability Zones with a load balancer and Auto Scaling keeps serving traffic when one AZ fails — the load balancer routes around unhealthy targets and Auto Scaling replaces capacity. Single-AZ designs, vertical scaling, and manual cross-region failover don't solve an AZ-level failure automatically.

choices: S3 Standard in one AZ
EBS snapshots copied manually each night
S3 with Cross-Region Replication (CRR)
EFS in a single AZ

RPO: 15 minutes. RTO: 1 hour.
Threat model: full region loss.

scenarios.situation: Compliance requires surviving a full region loss with at most 15 minutes of data loss and 1-hour recovery.
scenarios.title: Surviving a region loss
scenarios.why: S3 with Cross-Region Replication asynchronously replicates objects to another region, surviving region loss with a low RPO. S3 is already regional (data is stored across AZs); EBS/EFS are AZ-scoped without replication, and manual snapshots can't meet a 15-minute RPO reliably.

choices: An SQS queue between the API and the workers
Direct synchronous calls with retries
A larger worker fleet with no queue
Sticky sessions on the ALB

Flash sale: 50x normal traffic for 20 min.
Workers OOM'd; orders lost.
Traffic then flat for hours.
scenarios.hint: What absorbs a burst so nothing is lost when consumers can't keep up?

scenarios.situation: A flash sale sends 50x normal traffic for 20 minutes; synchronous workers are overwhelmed and orders are lost.
scenarios.title: Decoupling the flash sale
scenarios.why: An SQS queue decouples producers from consumers: the API accepts orders into a durable queue and workers drain it at their own pace — no orders lost during bursts. Synchronous calls couple failure modes; bigger fleets still can't handle arbitrary spikes without a buffer.

A bigger instance in the primary region
DNS TTL set to 24 hours for stability

SLO: 99.9% monthly (~43 min downtime).
Current: single-region active-passive
with manual failover (2h RTO).

choices: Deploy with rolling updates behind the ALB, keeping old instances until new ones pass health checks
Deploy to all instances simultaneously at 3 AM
Take the ALB out of service during deploys
Deploy to a single instance and copy its disk to the others

Last deploy: all instances replaced at once.
Bad build took the site down for 40 min.
Rollback required a full re-deploy.
scenarios.hint: What keeps serving traffic while the new version proves itself?
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment strategy prevents the next all-at-once outage?
scenarios.situation: A deploy replaced all instances simultaneously; a bad build caused a 40-minute outage with a painful rollback.
scenarios.title: Never deploy to everything at once
scenarios.why: Rolling updates (or blue/green) keep the old version serving behind the load balancer until new instances pass health checks, so a bad build never takes all capacity at once and rollback is instant. Simultaneous replacement maximizes blast radius; removing the ALB or disk-copying are fragile anti-patterns.

scenarios.title: Unhealthy Targets After Deploy
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce site on EC2 behind an ALB went down right after a deployment. Instances run fine and the app responds to curl on localhost, but the ALB marks every target unhealthy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the best next step?
choices: Update the target group health check path or make the app return 200 on /health
Replace the ALB with an NLB — the load balancer type is causing the failures
Double the instance size — unhealthy targets mean underpowered instances
Open the instance security groups to 0.0.0.0/0 — the ALB cannot reach the instances
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The deployment changed /health to return a 301 redirect; ALB expects HTTP 200 from the health check path Update the target group health check path or make the app return 200 on /health The distractors fail because: Replace the ALB with an NLB — the load balancer type is causing the failures does not address the observed symptom (All targets unhealthy: health check failed, got 301); Double the instance size — unhealthy targets mean underpowered instances is a valid practice but would not resolve this specific failure; Open the instance security groups to 0 treats a symptom rather than the cause.
scenarios.hint: Check what the health check actually receives versus what it expects.
objectives: Distinguish app issues from infrastructure issues
evidence: All targets unhealthy: health check failed, got 301

scenarios.title: Troubleshooting: Auto Scaling Groups and Scaling Policies
scenarios.situation: After a change involving auto scaling groups and scaling policies, users report degraded behavior. Reviewing the implementation, you find the team fell into a known trap: Using simple scaling for fast-changing metrics — it needs cooldowns and lags; target tracking or step scaling respond better. Background: An ASG maintains desired capacity across AZs using a launch template, scaling policies, and health checks (EC2 status + ELB + custom).
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the best next step?
choices: Remediate the root cause: An ASG maintains desired capacity across AZs using a launch template, scaling policies, and health checks (EC2 status + ELB + custom). Then verify with the checks from training.
Treat the symptom: forgetting multi-az: an asg in one az is not highly available no matter the instance count.
Increase capacity — bigger resources fix most issues
Roll back the monitoring — alerts are the problem, not the system
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The observed trap (Using simple scaling for fast-changing metrics — it needs cooldowns and lags; target tracking or step scaling respond better.) directly explains the degradation: An ASG maintains desired capacity across AZs using a launch template, scaling policies, and health checks (EC2 status + ELB + custom). Target tracking (e.g., 50% CPU) is the default right answer for steady scaling; step scaling reacts to CloudWatch alarm breaches with sized steps; scheduled scaling handles known patterns. The distractors treat symptoms, add cost without diagnosis, or remove visibility.
scenarios.hint: Connect the observed trap to the lesson's first key concept.
objectives: Diagnose Auto Scaling Groups and Scaling Policies failures
evidence: Degradation began after the change; implementation shows: Using simple scaling for fast-changing metrics — it needs cooldowns and lags; target tracking or step scaling respond better.
An ASG maintains desired capacity across AZs using a launch template, scaling policies, and health checks (EC2 status + ELB + custom).

scenarios.title: Compare: Load Balancers: ALB, NLB, and GWLB Approaches
scenarios.situation: Two engineers propose different approaches to load balancers: alb, nlb, and gwlb. Engineer A proposes: ALB (Layer 7): HTTP/HTTPS routing by path/host/header, target groups, WebSocket/gRPC, slow-start, sticky sessions. The default for web apps. Engineer B proposes: using CLB (classic) in new designs — it is legacy; ALB/NLB replace it. Context: GWLB: transparent insertion of third-party appliances (firewalls) via GENEVE encapsulation — the exam's 'inline inspection' answer.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach should you choose, and why?
choices: Engineer A — ALB (Layer 7): HTTP/HTTPS routing by path/host/header, target groups, WebSocket/gRPC, slow-start, sticky sessions. The default for web apps. NLB (Layer 4): ultra-low latency, static IPs/Elastic IPs, millions of RPS, preserves source IP. For TCP/UDP extremes and fixed IPs.
Engineer B — Using CLB (classic) in new designs — it is legacy; ALB/NLB replace it.
Neither — both approaches are equally valid; choose by coin flip
Combine them — take the easy parts of each
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Engineer A's approach implements the documented best practice: ALB (Layer 7): HTTP/HTTPS routing by path/host/header, target groups, WebSocket/gRPC, slow-start, sticky sessions. The default for web apps. NLB (Layer 4): ultra-low latency, static IPs/Elastic IPs, millions of RPS, preserves source IP. For TCP/UDP extremes and fixed IPs. Engineer B's shortcut is the exact pitfall training warns against: Using CLB (classic) in new designs — it is legacy; ALB/NLB replace it.
scenarios.hint: Match each proposal against the lesson's concepts and pitfalls.
objectives: Evaluate Load Balancers: ALB, NLB, and GWLB approaches
evidence: ALB (Layer 7): HTTP/HTTPS routing by path/host/header, target groups, WebSocket/gRPC, slow-start, sticky sessions. The default for web apps.
Using CLB (classic) in new designs — it is legacy; ALB/NLB replace it.

Switch to a larger single database instance
Move the database to S3

EBS io2 with provisioned IOPS
Instance store
EFS

scenarios.title: Troubleshooting: ElastiCache: Redis and Memcached
scenarios.situation: After a change involving elasticache: redis and memcached, users report degraded behavior. Reviewing the implementation, you find the team fell into a known trap: Caching without TTL — stale data forever; always set expiry unless you have invalidation logic. Background: Managed in-memory caching: Redis (persistent, pub/sub, sorted sets, cluster mode) vs Memcached (simple, multithreaded, no persistence).
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the best next step?
choices: Remediate the root cause: Managed in-memory caching: Redis (persistent, pub/sub, sorted sets, cluster mode) vs Memcached (simple, multithreaded, no persistence). Then verify with the checks from training.
Treat the symptom: choosing memcached when you need persistence or pub/sub — that is redis.
Increase capacity — bigger resources fix most issues
Roll back the monitoring — alerts are the problem, not the system
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The observed trap (Caching without TTL — stale data forever; always set expiry unless you have invalidation logic.) directly explains the degradation: Managed in-memory caching: Redis (persistent, pub/sub, sorted sets, cluster mode) vs Memcached (simple, multithreaded, no persistence). Patterns: lazy loading (cache-aside), write-through, TTL expiry. Redis Cluster mode shards data; Global Datastore replicates cross-region. The distractors treat symptoms, add cost without diagnosis, or remove visibility.
scenarios.hint: Connect the observed trap to the lesson's first key concept.
objectives: Diagnose ElastiCache: Redis and Memcached failures

concepts: ElastiCache (Redis) absorbs repeated reads in memory with sub-millisecond latency, collapsing both DB load and p99.

example.walkthrough: ElastiCache (Redis) absorbs repeated reads in memory with sub-millisecond latency, collapsing both DB load and p99. Read replicas still query disk-backed engines per request; vertical scaling is costly and doesn't fix the repeated-read pattern; S3 isn't a low-latency cache.

pitfalls: Common trap: EBS gp3 with default settings.
Common trap: EBS io2 with provisioned IOPS.
Common trap: switch to a larger single database instance.
Common trap: direct Connect for end users.

lessons.title: Secure Architectures — Core concepts
concepts: VPC endpoints (gateway or interface) keep traffic to AWS services on the AWS network from private subnets. SSE-S3 offers no key control or audit; client-side keys in a repo are a breach waiting to happen; a private VPC doesn't encrypt data at rest.
Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl.

Security groups (stateful, attached to instances/ENIs) and NACLs (stateless, attached to subnets) are complementary layers: NACLs provide coarse subnet guardrails, security groups provide precise instance rules.
KMS with customer managed keys provides key policies (separation of duties), automatic rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every key use.

example.code:
DB password: hardcoded in 14 repos.
Rotation: manual, last done 2022.
example.walkthrough: Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl. Environment variables and config files still leak; S3 is storage, not a secrets lifecycle service.

pitfalls: Common trap: security groups (stateful, instance-level).
Common trap: a public subnet with a security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0.
Common trap: store secrets in environment variables.
Common trap: client-side encryption with keys in the repo.

lessons.title: Cost-Optimized Architectures — Core concepts
concepts: Spot Instances offer deep discounts for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch rendering with checkpointing. Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility.

Cost optimization: NAT instances trade one cost for ops burden; public subnets break the security model; accepting the cost ignores the obvious fix. Multi-region for a single-region app adds cost, not savings.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent/infrequent/archive tiers based on observed access — ideal when patterns are unknown or changing.
Baseline vs peak: all On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.
NAT gateway costs: VPC endpoints route S3/DynamoDB traffic privately, bypassing NAT Gateway data-processing charges entirely (gateway endpoints are free).

example.code:
Web tier: 40 instances baseline 24/7.
Peaks: 120 instances, 4h/day.
example.walkthrough: Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility. All On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.

pitfalls: Common trap: savings Plans covering peak capacity.
Common trap: keep the NAT gateway and accept the cost.
Common trap: VPC endpoints for the AWS services the workloads call.
Common trap: reserved Instances for the batch workers.

lessons.title: Compute — Core concepts
concepts: Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. A single instance can't scale; Lambda/Fargate lack the networking and duration profile for tightly-coupled MPI.

Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs. Self-managed EC2 maximizes ops; Lambda doesn't fit a traditional long-running web server model as simply; Lightsail is simpler but less integrated for managed app environments.

Auto Scaling policies: baking dependencies into an AMI (automated with EC2 Image Builder) makes launches fast and consistent; Auto Scaling then reacts quickly. Target tracking policies continuously adjust capacity to keep the chosen metric (ALB request count per target) at the target value — ideal for a request-driven goal.
Image Builder: manual image copies don't scale; boot-time installs are the root cause; a single instance has no scaling at all.
Systems Manager Session Manager provides audited shell access to private instances with no bastion hosts, no public IPs, and no open inbound ports — logged to CloudTrail/S3.

example.code:
Video transcode: 45-90 min per file.
Queue-driven, containerized already.
example.walkthrough: Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs.

pitfalls: Common trap: EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling.
Common trap: private subnets with NAT + security groups allowing only needed ports.
Common trap: golden image copied manually to each instance.
Common trap: user data that apt-gets everything at boot (20 min boot).

lessons.title: Storage & Database — Core concepts
concepts: Aurora's storage-decoupled architecture supports up to 15 read replicas behind a reader endpoint, scaling PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible reads horizontally. RDS replicas are relational overhead for key-value; cache-only loses durability; Aurora Serverless v1 pauses and has scaling latency unsuited to 10x spikes.
Read scaling: multi-AZ alone adds a standby, not read scale; DynamoDB isn't relational; Redshift is analytics.
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM: objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires.
Instance store provides physically-attached NVMe storage with extreme IOPS and sub-ms latency at no extra cost — ideal for ephemeral scratch rebuilt from durable S3.
Ephemeral storage: dynamoDB provides durable managed key-value storage that scales to spikes, and DAX adds a microsecond in-memory cache in front.

example.code:
Regulator: financial records immutable
for 7 years, not even by admins.
example.walkthrough: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM: objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires. Versioning alone doesn't prevent deletion; EBS snapshots can be deleted; Glacier without Object Lock is just cheap storage.

pitfalls: Common trap: amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) policies.
Common trap: glacier Deep Archive without lock.
Common trap: EBS snapshots with no tested restore procedure — an untested backup is a hope, not a plan.

lessons.title: AWS Solutions Architect — Core concepts
concepts: Design VPCs in tiers: public subnets hold only internet-facing entry points (load balancers), private subnets hold app and data tiers, and NAT gateways per AZ give private resources safe outbound access. Security groups (stateful, instance-level) beat NACLs (stateless, subnet-level) for most filtering.

Build for AZ failure, not instance failure: load balancers and Auto Scaling groups span AZs, RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby, and S3 is AZ-redundant by default. If one building can take you down, the design is incomplete.

Choose the load balancer by protocol: ALB for HTTP/HTTPS with content-based routing, NLB for TCP/UDP with static IPs and extreme performance, GWLB for inserting network appliances. There is no universal balancer.

Tier S3 storage to access patterns with lifecycle policies — Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, and the Glacier family trade retrieval speed for price. Paying Standard rates for data you never read is the most common storage waste.

Pick data stores by access pattern: RDS/Aurora when you need SQL, joins, and transactions; DynamoDB when you need key-value scale at single-digit milliseconds; Redshift for analytics; ElastiCache to shed read load. One database rarely serves every pattern well.
Decouple with queues and events: SQS buffers work between tiers, SNS/EventBridge fan out notifications, and async boundaries let each tier scale and fail independently.

example.code:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc123def456 \
  --query 'RouteTables[*].{Subnet:Associations[0].SubnetId,Routes:Routes[*].DestinationCidrBlock}'
example.walkthrough: Inspecting route tables shows which subnets are truly public (a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway) versus private. Architects verify this before trusting any diagram — a 'private' subnet with an IGW route is public.

pitfalls: Common trap: one NAT gateway per VPC — if its AZ fails, every private subnet loses outbound access; use one per AZ.
Common trap: enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication and calling it a backup — replication copies objects, it does not protect against deletion without versioning and Object Lock.
Common trap: ALB for non-HTTP workloads — ALB only speaks Layer 7; TCP/UDP services need NLB.
Common trap: designing single-AZ 'to save money' while the business cannot tolerate the resulting downtime window.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Aws Saa move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.
